bibliographic.abstract: Decoherence remains a critical obstacle to achieving high-fidelity, scalable superconducting qubits, with the tunnel barrier of Josephson junctions a key source of loss. Here we apply resonant X- ray reflectivity to non-destructively probe the electronic structure of buried layers in Al/AlO _x_ /Al Josephson junctions. At the Al _K_ -edge, energy-dependent modulations in the reflectivity maps enable Kramers–Kronig–constrained extraction of the layer-resolved atomic scattering factors. The analysis reveals that the barrier coordination evolves from more tetrahedral toward predominantly octahedral character with increasing oxidation pressure. At the interfaces, the lower metal–oxide boundary is comparatively under-coordinated and disordered relative to the upper interface. Comparison with simulated X-ray absorption spectra identifies the dominant coordination motifs within the oxide and its interfaces, providing depth-resolved structural insight that constrains microscopic models of two-level system formation. These results link growth conditions, local coordination environments, and junction electronic properties, demonstrating resonant X-ray reflectivity as a powerful tool for probing the microscopic materials properties of Josephson junctions and providing a materials-level framework for mitigating decoherence in superconducting qubits.

XAS spectra acquired in total electron yield (TEY) mode at the Al K-edge.
Energy loss near-edge structure (ELNES) measurements at the Al L2,3 and O K edges.
Current-voltage measurements to extract junction barrier height and thickness using the Simmons tunneling model.
